newsitem.title: UK: Britain urges Israel, PLO to show "statesmanship".
newsitem.headline: Britain urges Israel, PLO to show "statesmanship".

text.p: Britain expressed grave concern on Thursday at the upsurge of violence on the West Bank and Gaza Strip and urged Israeli and Palestinian leaders to show "statesmanship" to halt the fighting.
The Foreign Office said fighting, in which 33 Palestinians and 10 Israelis have died, had left the Middle East peace process in a precarious state.

"Actions such as the opening of the tunnel along the Western Wall and the recent demolition of a Palestinian community centre in Jerusalem have cause suspicion and disquiet," the Foreign Office said in a statement.
"We call on Israeli and Palestinian leaders to exercise the statesmanship required and to step back from confrontation and return to the past of trust and reconciliation."
Reflecting the acute anxiety in Britain, Prime Minister John Major sent messages to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat urging restraint.
His office said he also telephoned Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and sent a message to Jordan's King Hussein.
A Foreign Office spokesman referred to Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind's comments on Wednesday in which he expressed concern about the impact of the violence on the Middle East peace process.
"It is very worrying, very disturbing," Rifkind told CNN.
"It is going to be very, very important to give the reassurance and to give the signs of tangible progress that can reduce the temperature and get matters under an even keel."
Rifkind said it was important that Netanyahu had met Arafat, establishing a personal relationship. But he said there was a need for progress in three crucial areas:
-- opening up Palestinian areas sealed off by Israel with "very disturbing" economic consequences.
-- redeployment of Israeli troops from the West Bank town of Hebron, as foreseen in interim peace agreements signed by the previous Israeli government.
-- a resumption of Israeli-Syrian peace talks, crucial to a comprehensive settlement in the region.
Rifkind said Britain had recognised a need for a "period of quiet reflection" for Netanyahu, who took office in June, to establish his government's position on a range of issues.

But he added: "Now you can't have that going on indefinitely. There is a momentum to the peace process and I think there is now a renewed sense of urgency that Mr Netanyahu's government must spell out the Israeli position and actually enter into the negotiations in a constructive way.
"I think that is what they want to do but I am not yet persuaded that they have clarified even in their own minds exactly what their strategic objectives might be."
